highlights.content: [IBM Newsroom](index.php) # All press releases # llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale • llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads. • llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads [1] and three times greater output throughput. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: * **Multi-tenant quality of service** — Priority and fairness-aware flow control helps latency-sensitive requests, and bursty agent workloads share a fleet without starving one another. * **Zero-downtime operations** — Router high availability with hot standby and rolling updates keep traffic flowing through upgrades and planned maintenance. highlights.content: [IBM Newsroom](index.php) # All press releases # llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale • llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads. • llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads [1] and three times greater output throughput. [2] Oct 20, 2026 ![](/image/iso_banner.png) **SAN JOSE, C.A., OCT. 20, 2026** – Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: * **Multi-tenant quality of service** — Priority and fairness-aware flow control helps latency-sensitive requests, and bursty agent workloads share a fleet without starving one another. * **Zero-downtime operations** — Router high availability with hot standby and rolling updates keep traffic flowing through upgrades and planned maintenance. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # VS Code 1.137 Puts AI Agents in Dev Containers [2026] ![Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 15 min read Microsoft has quietly turned its most popular code editor into something closer to an operating system for AI agents. Visual Studio Code 1.137, released September 9, 2026, and the follow-up update that landed roughly a week later, add a feature Microsoft calls the Agent Host system: an architecture that lets multiple AI coding agents run as managed processes inside the editor, each with its own isolated Dev Container, its own tools, and its own dependencies. Paired with new automations and a voice mode, the release marks the clearest sign yet that Microsoft sees the editor’s future as a control center for autonomous software work, not just a faster autocomplete box. The timing matters. The update landed in the same month Google opened Gemini 4 Argon to public developer access, OpenAI pushed GPT-6 Astra’s programming-language coverage past 87%, and DeepSeek shipped a coding-focused model built for end-to-end project work. VS Code’s agent infrastructure isn’t arriving in a vacuum. It’s arriving right as the underlying models get cheap and capable enough to actually run unattended for long stretches, which is the whole point of giving them a container to live in. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What the Agent Host System Actually Does According to the [official VS Code 1.137 release notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_137), the update reworks how the editor manages AI-driven processes. Instead of treating an AI coding assistant as a single chat panel bolted onto the sidebar, the Agent Host system gives each agent session its own managed runtime. That runtime can be spun up, paused, monitored, and torn down independently of the editor’s main process, which is the kind of plumbing you’d expect from a container orchestrator, not a text editor. Developer coverage of the release, including a [write-up on DEV Community](https://dev.to/hamidrazadev/vs-code-1137-is-here-automations-voice-mode-and-the-features-thatll-change-how-you-code-lgg), frames 1.137 as pushing the editor “closer to a real AI-powered coding partner” rather than a passive tool. The practical upshot: a developer can now kick off a background agent to refactor a module, keep working in the foreground on something else, and check back on the agent’s progress without losing their own editor state. ## Agents Now Run Inside Dev Containers The headline technical change is that agents can run inside local Dev Containers, each preloaded with the project’s own tools and dependencies. That’s a meaningful shift from running an agent directly against a developer’s host machine. A Dev Container gives the agent a sandboxed, reproducible environment that matches the project’s actual build and test setup, rather than whatever happens to be installed globally on the developer’s laptop. Industry analysis published around the update, including a piece from [Analytics Insight](https://www.analyticsinsight.net/artificial-intelligence/how-ai-is-changing-code-editors-in-2026), describes this as part of a broader pattern: “code editors become agent workspaces” where “one editor can handle many agents” at once. That framing lines up with what Microsoft shipped. The container boundary isn’t just a convenience, it’s a safety mechanism. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # GoTo’s 27B AI Model Targets 5 Indonesian Languages [2026] ![Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 17 min read PT GoTo Gojek Tokopedia Tbk unveiled a new 27-billion-parameter open-source language model in Sanur, Bali, on October 19, 2026, pushing deeper into a market that global AI labs have mostly treated as an afterthought: Indonesia’s regional languages. The model understands Bahasa Indonesia alongside Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, and Bataknese, and GoTo says it will stay free for startups, businesses, universities, researchers, and public institutions to use, study, and adapt. The release matters beyond Jakarta’s tech scene. Indonesia is home to more than 700 living languages, yet almost every major [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) from OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic treats Bahasa Indonesia as a secondary training target and regional dialects as an afterthought at best. GoTo’s new model, part of its [Sahabat-AI open-source ecosystem](https://www.gotocompany.com/en/news/press/indosat-ooredoo-hutchison-and-goto-launch-sahabat-ai-indonesias-open-source-llm-for-empowering-digital-sovereignty), is a bet that local context and cultural nuance can be a competitive edge global labs cannot easily replicate. This is not GoTo’s first swing at the problem. The company has been building toward this moment since late 2024, and the October 19 announcement marks the most ambitious version of that project yet. On October 20, 2026, the Chinese AI company released **DeepInfer**, described as its in-house inference framework, as free and open-source code under the Apache 2.0 license. The move, first flagged widely after [Gizmodo reported it as DeepSeek “dialing up the pressure” on OpenAI and Anthropic](https://gizmodo.com/deepseek-dials-up-the-pressure-on-openai-and-anthropic-with-open-source-inference-tool-2000828261), hands outside developers a working copy of the engine DeepSeek uses to serve its own models at scale, rather than just another research paper or weights dump. The release is narrow by design. DeepInfer currently supports only one model, **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, and it ships as offline inference software rather than a finished managed cloud product. But the symbolism is hard to miss: a company based in Hangzhou, formally named **Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd.**, is now giving away the exact kind of production-serving code that OpenAI and Anthropic have kept locked inside their own data centers. For a US and global audience watching the AI infrastructure race, that is the story worth unpacking. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. That license matters: it is one of the most permissive open-source terms available, allowing commercial use, modification, and redistribution without requiring the resulting product to be open-sourced in turn. Alongside DeepInfer, DeepSeek also published a smaller companion project called **deepseek-recipe**. That component handles token encoding and decoding, and its processing logic is aligned with the official DeepSeek API, meaning developers who self-host DeepInfer can expect the same tokenization behavior they would get calling DeepSeek’s hosted service. DeepSeek has said inference code for future models will continue to be added to the DeepInfer repository over time, suggesting this is the first entry in an ongoing release schedule rather than a one-off gesture. Visual Studio Code 1.137, released September 9, 2026, and the follow-up update that landed roughly a week later, add a feature Microsoft calls the Agent Host system: an architecture that lets multiple AI coding agents run as managed processes inside the editor, each with its own isolated Dev Container, its own tools, and its own dependencies. Paired with new automations and a voice mode, the release marks the clearest sign yet that Microsoft sees the editor’s future as a control center for autonomous software work, not just a faster autocomplete box. The timing matters. The update landed in the same month Google opened Gemini 4 Argon to public developer access, OpenAI pushed GPT-6 Astra’s programming-language coverage past 87%, and DeepSeek shipped a coding-focused model built for end-to-end project work. VS Code’s agent infrastructure isn’t arriving in a vacuum. It’s arriving right as the underlying models get cheap and capable enough to actually run unattended for long stretches, which is the whole point of giving them a container to live in. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What the Agent Host System Actually Does According to the [official VS Code 1.137 release notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_137), the update reworks how the editor manages AI-driven processes. Instead of treating an AI coding assistant as a single chat panel bolted onto the sidebar, the Agent Host system gives each agent session its own managed runtime. That runtime can be spun up, paused, monitored, and torn down independently of the editor’s main process, which is the kind of plumbing you’d expect from a container orchestrator, not a text editor. Developer coverage of the release, including a [write-up on DEV Community](https://dev.to/hamidrazadev/vs-code-1137-is-here-automations-voice-mode-and-the-features-thatll-change-how-you-code-lgg), frames 1.137 as pushing the editor “closer to a real AI-powered coding partner” rather than a passive tool. The practical upshot: a developer can now kick off a background agent to refactor a module, keep working in the foreground on something else, and check back on the agent’s progress without losing their own editor state. ## Agents Now Run Inside Dev Containers The headline technical change is that agents can run inside local Dev Containers, each preloaded with the project’s own tools and dependencies. That’s a meaningful shift from running an agent directly against a developer’s host machine. A Dev Container gives the agent a sandboxed, reproducible environment that matches the project’s actual build and test setup, rather than whatever happens to be installed globally on the developer’s laptop. Industry analysis published around the update, including a piece from [Analytics Insight](https://www.analyticsinsight.net/artificial-intelligence/how-ai-is-changing-code-editors-in-2026), describes this as part of a broader pattern: “code editors become agent workspaces” where “one editor can handle many agents” at once. That framing lines up with what Microsoft shipped. The container boundary isn’t just a convenience, it’s a safety mechanism. The company first announced the project in June, building in support for spending controls alongside card, bank account, and stablecoin payments. Mastercard demonstrated the system at Cloudflare Connect, where marketing agency Hype assigned an AI agent to prepare a campaign for a protein bar launch. The agent bought social media research from AIsa and ordered eight campaign images from Cloudflare AI Gateway, all within a budget Hype had approved, completing nine total payments across the two providers. **Why Coinbase and Base Handle the Crypto Side** The agent paid using Coinbase’s x402 protocol, a system that lets websites and AI agents request and send payments automatically, without a human clicking “buy.” When a merchant needed payment, the system flagged it, checked that the agent’s payment was valid, then released the service. Mastercard said these payments can be grouped together and settled later instead of handling each one separately. Coinbase supplied the digital wallet that funded the agent during the test, while Base, Coinbase’s own blockchain, handled the actual transfer of funds. BVNK, a stablecoin payments company Mastercard bought in August, managed the agent’s wallet and processed the payments through Mastercard’s existing payment network, in either regular currency or stablecoins. Sellers could choose how they wanted to get paid. “The web gave software a way to communicate. APIs gave software a way to use services. Now AI agents need a way to pay for them,” Mastercard said. “That’s what we’re building.” **Where MA Stands Technically** Mastercard shares rose nearly 1% to $621 Monday, testing rising trendline resistance near $624 to $625 after a sharp October rally. AI Agents.content: [Accessibility Statement](https://www.cision.com/about/accessibility/) [Skip Navigation](#main) # Rhapsody Launches Guardian to Govern AI Agent and API Access to Healthcare Data and Services [![Rhapsody logo]( "Rhapsody logo")](#) --- ## News provided by [**Rhapsody**](/news/rhapsody/) Oct 20, 2026, 08:00 ET ## Share this article Share toX ![]() Share this article Share toX ![]() --- *Helps health systems put CHAI and Joint Commission guidance into practice by providing access controls and audit trails for AI agents and APIs.* BOSTON, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- [Rhapsody](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4799731-1&h=2391572119&u=https%3A%2F%2Frhapsody.health%2F&a=Rhapsody), a provider of infrastructure and automation for agentic interoperability, today announced [Rhapsody® Guardian](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4799731-1&h=2749521984&u=https%3A%2F%2Frhapsody.health%2Fsolutions%2Fguardian%2F&a=Rhapsody%C2%AE+Guardian), an AI governance solution that helps healthcare organizations enforce AI governance policies by controlling how AI agents access health data and services. Unveiled at Rhapsody's customer conference, [Connect](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4799731-1&h=1066188502&u=https%3A%2F%2Frhapsody.health%2Fresources%2Fconnect-developer-conference%2F&a=Connect), in Boston, Guardian addresses a growing challenge for health systems: translating AI governance policies into controls over what agents can access and do. It authenticates agents, enforces scoped access and rate limits, and records agent, MCP, and API activity, helping organizations advance AI initiatives while maintaining oversight of sensitive healthcare data. For example, a health system can authorize an agent to access a designated service, restrict it to permitted operations, and limit how frequently it can make requests. Guardian enforces these boundaries and maintains an audit trail of activity passing through it. "CIOs are under pressure to advance AI initiatives while maintaining control of sensitive healthcare data," said Sagnik Bhattacharya, CEO of Rhapsody. "They need to know which agents are accessing their systems, what those agents are allowed to do and whether they stay within those boundaries. Guardian puts their decisions into practice, helping health systems move from AI policy to controlled deployment." Organizations can deploy Guardian independently or alongside Rhapsody, Corepoint or another integration platform. This flexibility gives health systems a central point for enforcing access policies. Guardian is available now. For more information, or to schedule a demo, visit [Rhapsody.Health](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4799731-1&h=2513111862&u=https%3A%2F%2Frhapsody.health%2Fget-a-demo%2F&a=Rhapsody.Health). Editor's Note: A high-resolution image of the Rhapsody Guardian dashboard is available [here](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4799731-1&h=1301887568&u=https%3A%2F%2Frhapsody.health%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F10%2FRhapsody-Guardian-Product-Preview.jpg&a=here). **About Rhapsody**Rhapsody provides healthcare interoperability and automation solutions that help organizations connect systems, govern data access and do more with the teams they have. Its portfolio spans integration, identity, clinical terminology, AI governance and interoperability automation, helping healthcare organizations adopt new technology while building on the systems they already use. Learn more at rhapsody.health. Image: MiniMax China’s MiniMax is taking aim at the cost of autonomous AI, introducing a new model it says can handle agent tasks faster and more cheaply than its predecessor. The company launched M3.1 Flash on Monday, claiming the model operates nearly three times faster than its previous version while reducing agent task costs by 70%. MiniMax also revealed that its anonymously tested model, known as “Space Bunny,” had processed more than 200 trillion tokens before the official release. The launch adds another low-cost contender to the increasingly competitive AI model market. But independent evaluations raise an important question for businesses: whether lower inference costs can offset the additional work needed to verify an agent’s output. ## Benchmarks and the price ledger Available immediately through MiniMax’s API, desktop coding environment, and subscription plans, M3.1 Flash targets multi-step enterprise workflows. MiniMax prices standard input tokens at $0.15 per million, output at $0.60 per million, and cached reads at $0.015 per million. [The vendor highlights competitive parity](https://www.minimax.io/blog/minimax-m31f) with leading frontier systems on specialized agent benchmarks. On Automation-Bench v1.0.6, M3.1 Flash posted a 62.8 score across 600 multi-application business workflows, edging out DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017’s 60.5. It also scored 76.2 on BankerToolBench, tying [Claude Opus 5](https://www.techrepublic.com/article/news-anthropic-claude-opus-5-5-pricing-performance/) on financial compliance and chained tool executions. On OSWorld 2.0, it logged 61.7, leading domestic Chinese rivals. Independent [evaluations from Artificial Analysis](https://x.com/ArtificialAnlys/status/2112211865128608002) gave M3.1 Flash an Intelligence Index score of 42 at maximum reasoning, bringing the evaluator’s average benchmark task cost down from $0.51 on M3 to approximately $0.22. ## Reliability gaps and hidden frictions Independent assessments reveal substantial operational hurdles. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand. Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization. In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents. The solution uses [Amazon Bedrock](/bedrock/) for LLM inference through the [AWS Strands Agents SDK](https://github.com/strands-agents/sdk-python). AI Agents.content: Advertisement For premium support please call: For premium support please call: # A flaw in three major AI agent platforms shows why guardrails don't work ![Stacker](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/aol_stacker_articles_387.png) ![A business professional operating multiple AI agent platforms and system robots in an organization. - tadamichi // Shutterstock](https://hermes.media.transform.aol.com/070e05aba59d03d0373d722e2efa0ad0f16427c0/w_1200,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/10/20/f1f314dd-ad44-37d8-8ff6-26758a5eadde/5d120ff1-0136-49a9-8547-9e50be64f8b4.jpg) At Black Hat 2026, researchers Aviyam Ivgi and Hedi Ingber showed one structural flaw running through three of the largest agent stacks: AWS Bedrock AgentCore with the Strands SDK, Google's Agent Development Kit, and Vercel's AI SDK harness. They named that flaw CoreBreak. AWS patched [CVE-2026-18830](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-18830) (CVSS 8.6), Google patched [CVE-2026-18236](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-18236) (CVSS 9.3, critical), and Vercel patched [CVE-2026-64650](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-64650) and [CVE-2026-64651](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-64651). All three vendors had put enforcement where the agent could reach it. The guardrails the industry relies on are all wrapped around the model: system prompts, content filters, refusal training. If you bypass the model, you bypass all of them. CoreBreak showed two ways to do exactly that: 1. Feed the harness a message history whose latest message already contains a tool call, and the tool runs with attacker-chosen arguments while the model and every guardrail wrapped around it never fires. 2. Forge an "approved" confirmation event in that same history, and the human-in-the-loop step approves an action that no human saw. The approval mechanism itself became the attack vector. As the AI infrastructure company [Redpanda](https://www.redpanda.com) explores, the emergency fixes all converged on the same move: bind tool execution to a state that the attacker cannot author, and reject externally supplied tool calls and approvals. That's called [out-of-band policy enforcement](https://www.redpanda.com/blog/agentic-ai-needs-out-of-band-governance), or OBPE, and each vendor had to rebuild a piece of it under fire, one patch at a time. ### The researchers already stated the fix The researchers' own hardening list reads like a description of OBPE. They called for rejecting caller-authored tool calls, authorizing at execution time, reducing inherited authority, and binding each tool invocation to the exact model event and authorization state that produced it. That is a specification for enforcement outside the agent. The industry's most effective red team and Redpanda’s own research group reached the same conclusion independently. The credential-theft path CoreBreak exposed is worth highlighting: Injected instructions steered managed browser and code-interpreter tools into reading the execution role's cloud credentials and exfiltrating them. No policy engine changes a sandbox's networking. The lesson is what you hand an agent in the first place. A typed, mediated tool grant keeps the credential behind the boundary. A general compute environment with ambient cloud credentials puts it one HTTP request away from any injected instruction. Advertisement ### Different research, same conclusion Redpanda [published its own research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27646) testing a comparable enforcement architecture against a related attack class: prompt-injected agents coaxed into leaking protected data or taking unauthorized actions. In its benchmark, the researchers ran 3,621 trials across four models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5, and GPT-5 mini) to measure this directly. Agents guarded only by prompt rules failed in 57.6% of trials, leaking protected data, revealing protected values, or completing forbidden backend effec...

LLMs.content: [IBM Newsroom](index.php) # All press releases # llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale • llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads. • llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads [1] and three times greater output throughput. [2] Oct 20, 2026 ![](/image/iso_banner.png) **SAN JOSE, C.A., OCT. 20, 2026** – Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: * **Multi-tenant quality of service** — Priority and fairness-aware flow control helps latency-sensitive requests, and bursty agent workloads share a fleet without starving one another. * **Zero-downtime operations** — Router high availability with hot standby and rolling updates keep traffic flowing through upgrades and planned maintenance. Management of prefill/decode replicas as one logical unit, with coordinated rollouts and lockstep upgrades—making disaggregated serving practical in production. * **A stable foundation to build on** — A v1 configuration API and a hardened request path, validated across clouds and accelerators, give adopters a release they can standardize on. * **Agent-aware serving** — Session-aware routing keeps multi-turn conversations close to their cached context, while turn-priority scheduling and native Responses API state support help agents reuse context a...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # DeepSeek Opens DeepInfer, Presses OpenAI, Anthropic [2026] ![Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp) [Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/) Updated Oct 21, 2026 · 15 min read DeepSeek has pulled back the curtain on the software that runs its own AI servers. On October 20, 2026, the Chinese AI company released **DeepInfer**, described as its in-house inference framework, as free and open-source code under the Apache 2.0 license. The move, first flagged widely after [Gizmodo reported it as DeepSeek “dialing up the pressure” on OpenAI and Anthropic](https://gizmodo.com/deepseek-dials-up-the-pressure-on-openai-and-anthropic-with-open-source-inference-tool-2000828261), hands outside developers a working copy of the engine DeepSeek uses to serve its own models at scale, rather than just another research paper or weights dump. The release is narrow by design. DeepInfer currently supports only one model, **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, and it ships as offline inference software rather than a finished managed cloud product. But the symbolism is hard to miss: a company based in Hangzhou, formally named **Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd.**, is now giving away the exact kind of production-serving code that OpenAI and Anthropic have kept locked inside their own data centers. For a US and global audience watching the AI infrastructure race, that is the story worth unpacking. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What DeepSeek Actually Released on October 20 DeepInfer is DeepSeek’s name for what the company calls its “in-house inference framework.” According to the official GitHub repository and companion documentation, the code was published on October 20, 2026, and immediately made available for anyone to download, inspect, and modify under the Apache 2.0 license. That license matters: it is one of the most permissive open-source terms available, allowing commercial use, modification, and redistribution without requiring the resulting product to be open-sourced in turn. Alongside DeepInfer, DeepSeek also published a smaller companion project called **deepseek-recipe**. That component handles token encoding and decoding, and its processing logic is aligned with the official DeepSeek API, meaning developers who self-host DeepInfer can expect the same tokenization behavior they would get calling DeepSeek’s hosted service. DeepSeek has said inference code for future models will continue to be added to the DeepInfer repository over time, suggesting this is the first entry in an ongoing release schedule rather than a one-off gesture. [SiliconANGLE’s coverage of the release](https://siliconangle.com/2026/10/20/deepseek-open-sources-deepinfer-the-inference-framework-behind-its-production-services/) frames DeepInfer specifically as “the inference framework behind its production services,” underlining that this is not a stripped-down demo but the same lineage of code DeepSeek uses to answer real customer traffic. That distinction, software built for a live production workload rather than a lab benchmark, is what separates this release from most open-source AI tooling. ## Inside DeepInfer: What the Framework Actually Does Documentation published with the release describes a set of capabilities aimed squarely at large-scale serving rather than single-GPU experimentation. DeepInfer supports distributed inference across multiple chips and machines, speculative decoding to speed up token generation, a technique DeepSeek calls “SWA bounded replay,” and structured outputs for applications that need predictable, machine-readable responses rather than freeform text. The move, first flagged widely after [Gizmodo reported it as DeepSeek “dialing up the pressure” on OpenAI and Anthropic](https://gizmodo.com/deepseek-dials-up-the-pressure-on-openai-and-anthropic-with-open-source-inference-tool-2000828261), hands outside developers a working copy of the engine DeepSeek uses to serve its own models at scale, rather than just another research paper or weights dump. The release is narrow by design. DeepInfer currently supports only one model, **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, and it ships as offline inference software rather than a finished managed cloud product. But the symbolism is hard to miss: a company based in Hangzhou, formally named **Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd.**, is now giving away the exact kind of production-serving code that OpenAI and Anthropic have kept locked inside their own data centers. For a US and global audience watching the AI infrastructure race, that is the story worth unpacking. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. That license matters: it is one of the most permissive open-source terms available, allowing commercial use, modification, and redistribution without requiring the resulting product to be open-sourced in turn. Alongside DeepInfer, DeepSeek also published a smaller companion project called **deepseek-recipe**. That component handles token encoding and decoding, and its processing logic is aligned with the official DeepSeek API, meaning developers who self-host DeepInfer can expect the same tokenization behavior they would get calling DeepSeek’s hosted service. DeepSeek has said inference code for future models will continue to be added to the DeepInfer repository over time, suggesting this is the first entry in an ongoing release schedule rather than a one-off gesture. [SiliconANGLE’s coverage of the release](https://siliconangle.com/2026/10/20/deepseek-open-sources-deepinfer-the-inference-framework-behind-its-production-services/) frames DeepInfer specifically as “the inference framework behind its production services,” underlining that this is not a stripped-down demo but the same lineage of code DeepSeek uses to answer real customer traffic. That distinction, software built for a live production workload rather than a lab benchmark, is what separates this release from most open-source AI tooling. ## Inside DeepInfer: What the Framework Actually Does Documentation published with the release describes a set of capabilities aimed squarely at large-scale serving rather than single-GPU experimentation. AI Product.content: UPDATED 08:00 EDT / OCTOBER 20 2026 ### AI startup Vectorial lands $3M in funding to simulate human behavior for consumer research Consumer research is a slow and cumbersome challenge that few companies do well, but if Vectorial AI Inc. is successful, they’ll never have to worry about doing it again. The startup today said it has raised $3 million in seed funding to propel the launch of its new artificial intelligence-driven platform that simulates human behavior to generate valuable feedback for product development and marketing teams. Today’s round was jointly led by Smilegate and SenseAI Ventures, with additional funding coming from the ecosystem funds of the University of California at Berkeley and Stanford University. Angel investors from Meta Platforms Inc., Mastercard Inc. and Shopify Inc. also contributed to the round. Vectorial believes it has identified a critical bottleneck in technology development. These days, virtually every company is using AI tools to generate massive amounts of code, accelerating the development of new software products and applications. But consumer research is still stuck in the dark ages. Most firms still rely on outdated surveys of real audiences, which can take weeks to compile and complete, and are usually very limited in scale, with perhaps only 50 to 100 participants. According to Vectorial co-founder and Chief Executive Taranveer Singh, many smaller startups simply avoid doing user research altogether, and just assume or hope they know what consumers actually want. But that’s hit-and-miss at best, and it leads to hours of wasted time and money spent on products no one needs. “We believe AI is creating two distinct frontiers,” Singh told SiliconANGLE. “One focuses on reasoning and solving complex problems, while the other focuses on simulations and decoding human behavior.” Rather than gather up real humans to test new products, Vectorial has built a platform that uses AI to simulate thousands of users within specified target demographics. It’s based on the concept of a “living model” of target customers that continuously updates itself to take into account emerging trends and behavioral shifts. Singh says the feedback generated from these simulated audiences is extremely accurate, and he’s convinced that this method will become the standard for all new consumer products within the next four years or so. “Two pieces are missing,” he said. “The ability to simulate many scenarios, and the ability to bring your users into the same room as you build.” Several other startups have tried to use AI to solve the consumer research conundrum before, but Singh believes that all of them have fallen short, because none of them actually models human behavior. One solution that’s been tried repeatedly is AI-moderated interviews, but these still take multiple days to organize because they’re still reliant on real humans, and they usually involve small sample sizes. Another popular approach is to use synthetic agents, but Singh says these lack grounding in real consumer behavior, which means their outputs can’t be trusted. So how does Vectorial improve on these methods? Its solution is to embed its simulated audiences directly into companies’ development workflows, so developers receive a continuous flow of feedback that informs all of their decisions. Vectorial’s platform is powered by a behavior model called SAPIENS, which is continuously being trained on latent socio-demographic, psychographic and behavioral traits across a mammoth database of more than 2.5 million real consumers. AI Product.content: CFOtech Asia - Technology news for CFOs & financial decision-makers [![CFOtech Asia logo](/brands/cfo-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access](https://cfotech.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/20/tony-mcmanus-story-321815.webp) [Data governance](https://cfotech.asia/tag/data-governance) [Risk & Compliance](https://cfotech.asia/tag/risk-compliance) [GenAI](https://cfotech.asia/tag/generative-ai) # Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access Wed, 21st Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://cfotech.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Bloomberg has launched Enterprise MCP for its Data Licence Plus service, designed to connect Bloomberg data with clients' artificial intelligence applications. The system gives AI agents access to licensed Bloomberg data through a standardised interface covering more than 100 million securities and over 50,000 fields. The offering is intended to address a problem that has emerged as financial firms test generative AI tools: models may be able to reason over information, but often lack enough context to interpret market and reference data correctly. Enterprise MCP is an access layer over Data Licence Plus, Bloomberg's newer Data Licence product. It combines metadata on data fields with semantic search tools and workflow-specific functions, allowing users to request information in natural language instead of relying on field codes or manual identifier matching. The service can provide details including what a data field represents, how it was calculated, when it applies, and qualifiers such as currency, exchange, price type, period and date. It also includes entity resolution tools designed to map names, tickers or descriptions to the correct instrument and its links to the issuing company. Bloomberg is offering the product as an enterprise service in which it hosts and manages the access layer, while clients retain control over the AI agents and applications connected to it, including the models, prompts and instructions used in their workflows. That structure reflects a broader approach emerging in financial services, where firms want to use large language models and agent-based systems but remain cautious about data governance, entitlements and audit requirements. Under the new service, Bloomberg validates a firm's entitlements before returning data in response to an agent request under standard Data Licence rights. Requests are resolved against Bloomberg's Operational Datastore, while tool-level limits cap the number of securities and fields returned in a single call. **Workflow focus** The initial release includes what Bloomberg calls workflow skills, or reusable procedures tied to common financial tasks. These cover point-in-time universe retrieval, corporate action adjustment and revision history. The first set of skills will also help users identify outliers in a group of tickers, review trades that breach accepted price deviation thresholds, and assess securities and trades for possible sanctions exposure. Bloomberg is presenting the service as a way to reduce manual steps in research, portfolio management, risk and operations. In practice, that means reducing the work involved in locating the right dataset, matching identifiers and checking whether a figure is fit for a given task. It has also become a SpaceXAI Partner Network Transformation Partner. The new product, Zetaris Cloud, is designed to let AI systems query enterprise data where it already sits across structured, unstructured and streaming sources, rather than requiring companies to move or duplicate that data first. The system applies security, policy and access controls to data wherever it is queried. Zetaris says this is intended to address a common obstacle in enterprise AI projects: models and agents can generate code quickly but still struggle to access current internal data safely. Vinay Samuel, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Zetaris, said the problem was slowing broader adoption of AI in business settings. "Coding harnesses have dramatically accelerated software development, but enterprise AI still struggles to access trustworthy, governed data," Samuel said. "Our AI Data Harness gives AI tools a real-time path to the data they need, wherever it lives, without forcing companies to centralize everything first." Zetaris Cloud offers the architecture as a cloud service, allowing customers to connect models and agents to existing data environments without committing to a single cloud provider, data platform or AI model. Zetaris also argued that reducing the need to copy and centralise data could lower infrastructure demand. Based on an internal customer assessment, it said the product could cut total cost of ownership by up to 67 per cent. **Partnership and testing** Alongside the product launch, Zetaris outlined a broader collaboration with SpaceXAI centred on a large online developer contest run by GenAI Works. More than 5,000 developers from over 100 countries are expected to take part, using SpaceXAI's Grok Build with the Zetaris AI Data Harness. The event is framed as a test of whether AI coding tools can be paired with direct access to distributed enterprise data in live development settings. Developers will build enterprise AI applications using both systems together. "Putting these technologies in the hands of thousands of developers will show what becomes possible when AI agents can work with live enterprise data without sacrificing security," Samuel said. "The hackathon is designed to move that idea from theory into working applications." SpaceXAI described the pairing as a combination of coding tools and governed data access. "A coding harness is an important part of building enterprise AI applications. Also very important is instant access to relevant, governed data-the role of a data harness. Through the hackathon, developers will explore how Grok Build and Zetaris can be used together to combine these two complementary harnesses to build AI-enabled workflows. We look forward to seeing what the developer community creates," Adams said. **Nouri joins** Nouri joins Zetaris while remaining Chief Executive Officer and Co-Found...

[2] Oct 20, 2026 ![](/image/iso_banner.png) **SAN JOSE, C.A., OCT. 20, 2026** – Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # GoTo’s 27B AI Model Targets 5 Indonesian Languages [2026] ![Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 17 min read PT GoTo Gojek Tokopedia Tbk unveiled a new 27-billion-parameter open-source language model in Sanur, Bali, on October 19, 2026, pushing deeper into a market that global AI labs have mostly treated as an afterthought: Indonesia’s regional languages. The model understands Bahasa Indonesia alongside Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, and Bataknese, and GoTo says it will stay free for startups, businesses, universities, researchers, and public institutions to use, study, and adapt. The release matters beyond Jakarta’s tech scene. Indonesia is home to more than 700 living languages, yet almost every major [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) from OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic treats Bahasa Indonesia as a secondary training target and regional dialects as an afterthought at best. GoTo’s new model, part of its [Sahabat-AI open-source ecosystem](https://www.gotocompany.com/en/news/press/indosat-ooredoo-hutchison-and-goto-launch-sahabat-ai-indonesias-open-source-llm-for-empowering-digital-sovereignty), is a bet that local context and cultural nuance can be a competitive edge global labs cannot easily replicate. This is not GoTo’s first swing at the problem. The company has been building toward this moment since late 2024, and the October 19 announcement marks the most ambitious version of that project yet. Here is what GoTo actually announced, what remains unconfirmed, and why the move fits a broader pattern of countries and companies racing to build their own “sovereign AI” rather than renting it from Silicon Valley. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The company’s official release describes the new system as a 27 billion parameter large language model, built to understand and generate text across Bahasa Indonesia and four regional languages: Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, and Bataknese. Indonesian outlet [Detik](https://inet.detik.com/cyberlife/d-8716074/goto-rilis-model-llm-27b-paham-bahasa-indonesia-hingga-daerah) reported on the launch, framing it as GoTo’s answer to a gap that general-purpose chatbots have struggled to close: understanding not just Bahasa Indonesia but the linguistic texture of the country’s regional tongues. Business outlet [Bisnis.com](https://teknologi.bisnis.com/read/20261019/266/2013711/goto-luncurkan-ai-llm-open-source-27-miliar-parameter-dari-bahasa-jawa-hingga-batak) similarly covered the release, noting the model spans everything from Javanese to Bataknese and ties into GoTo’s broader open-source AI ecosystem push. GoTo has positioned the release as freely available, meaning startups, businesses, universities, researchers, and public institutions can use, study, and adapt the model without the licensing friction that often comes with proprietary systems from Western AI labs. That framing echoes the open-weight strategy used by companies ranging from Mistral to DeepSeek, where releasing model weights publicly builds developer goodwill and distribution even without a direct revenue line from the model itself. Open Source AI.content: UPDATED 08:00 EDT / OCTOBER 20 2026 ### IBM-backed llm-d framework adds controls for running AI models in-house by Paul Gillin IBM Corp. and several other contributors to the open-source llm-d project are releasing version 1.0 of their distributed artificial intelligence inference framework, adding operational controls intended to help enterprises run large models reliably on their own infrastructure. The release, announced ahead of the PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose today and tomorrow, focuses on managing competing workloads, maintaining service during upgrades and improving hardware efficiency as AI agents generate growing volumes of model requests. Built for Kubernetes, llm-d coordinates model serving across computing infrastructure. IBM, its Red Hat subsidiary and Google LLC are its lead maintainers. They co-founded the project last year with CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia Corp. Other contributors include Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Cisco Systems Inc., Hugging Face Inc., Intel Corp. and Mistral AI SAS. The project offers organizations seeking more control over inference costs and infrastructure choices a way to reduce dependence on a single model provider, cloud or hardware platform. “At IBM Research, we are seeing that open large language models and llm-d can greatly lower the costs of inference in computationally demanding problems such as designing hardware for quantum error correction, helping achieve a 11.8X efficiency advantage,” Ruchir Puri, IBM Research’s chief scientist, vice president of IBM’s Technology & Technical Community and IBM Fellow, wrote in e-mailed comments. “Llm-d 1.0 extends these savings by delivering the operational readiness needed for enterprises to extract more out of their computational capacity.” The project is focused on what happens after deployment. A production inference service must handle changing traffic, hardware failures, software updates and users competing for resources while maintaining acceptable response times. Version 1.0 adds support for quality of service across multiple tenants, zero-downtime operations and serving patterns tailored to AI agents. Flow controls and prioritization are designed to keep bursts of agent activity from overwhelming services that require fast responses, such as coding assistants used by people. The release “adds the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable [application programming interface], multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure and upgrades that don’t interrupt operations,” said Carlos Costa, distinguished engineer at IBM Research and a project co-founder and lead maintainer. Workloads can behave differently even when they reach models through the same endpoint. An agent may issue many requests, pause to use an external tool and return for additional model calls. The framework can keep requests directed to appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns, increasing opportunities to reuse previously processed context. That matters because agents repeatedly consult the same code, documents, instructions and conversation history while completing assignments. A routing system directs requests toward replicas that already hold relevant cached context. Another capability moves cached information among graphics processing unit memory, CPU memory and storage, preserving reusable information when GPU capacity becomes constrained. These techniques were previously available, but version 1.0 integrates them with operational controls, along with methods that separate prompt processing from response generation, optimize work batches and distribute large mixture-of-experts models across accelerators. IBM cited a recent agentic coding test in which the framework’s router captured 97% of available cache reuse. Open Source AI.titleZh: llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for production - IBM Research
Open Source AI.content: 4 minute read # llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for day 2 production operations The distributed inference framework makes serving large models on your own infrastructure reliable and affordable for the agentic era. Today at the PyTorch Conference North America, llm-d project contributors are announcing llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for open-source AI infrastructure. A Kubernetes-native [distributed inference serving network](https://research.ibm.com/blog/distributed-inference), llm-d makes it possible to deploy inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud. The release signals that llm-d has moved beyond demonstrating individual performance techniques and is ready to support the realities of production: sustained efficiency under many workloads, all while balancing service priorities amid growing demand. And with inference costs increasing, llm-d is meant to help bring model deployment in-house and deliver returns on AI investment. The work has been developed with a growing open-source community that includes hardware providers, model developers, cloud platforms, and enterprise users. As lead maintainers of llm-d, Red Hat, IBM, and Google have helped turn advanced inference techniques into a coordinated system that enterprises can operate at scale. The three co-founded llm-d last year with CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and industry leaders including AMD, Cisco, Hugging Face, Intel, Lambda, and Mistral AI have joined as contributors along the way. The result is a vendor-neutral alternative for organizations that want frontier-class inference performance without depending entirely on one proprietary model provider, cloud, or hardware platform. “llm-d is ready for day 2 operations,” said Carlos Costa, Distinguished Engineer at IBM Research, llm-d co-founder and lead maintainer. “llm-d has been delivering state-of-the-art inference performance for production workloads. What 1.0 adds is the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable API, multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure, and upgrades that don't interrupt operations. That is what we built llm-d 1.0 to do.” ## A full production stack Since llm-d launched, the project has focused on five important approaches to improving AI inference: prefix-cache-aware routing, which directs a request to infrastructure that may already hold its shared context; KV-cache offloading, which expands the useful life of cached information by moving it across GPU, CPU, and storage resources; batch inference optimization, which groups work so infrastructure can process it more efficiently; prefill/decode disaggregation, which separates the work of reading a prompt from the work of generating a response; and wide expert parallelism, which distributes large mixture-of-experts models across many accelerators. These ideas are not new to version 1.0. What is new is the level of integration and operational maturity around them. With version 1.0, llm-d has matured into a stack capable of supporting day 2 operations: everything that must happen after an AI service is deployed. That includes serving workloads with competing priorities, managing different performance requirements, maintaining efficiency, prioritizing important services, and keeping the system dependable over time. A benchmark can show that one feature improves throughput, but a production system must keep delivering that performance when traffic changes, hardware fails, software is updated, or different users compete for the same resources. llm-d 1.0 is about making the individual techniques work together under those less predictable conditions. ## One endpoint, different kinds of work Expanding on the core technical innovations that have already made llm-d a powerful tool for distributed inference, llm-d 1.0 enhances support for multi-tenant quality of service, zero-downtime operations, and agent-aware serving, for sustained performance in common day 2 production operatio...

That includes serving workloads with competing priorities, managing different performance requirements, maintaining efficiency, prioritizing important services, and keeping the system dependable over time. [Helical Insight](https://www.helicalinsight.com/), an open-source BI platform that get’s installed on-premises, now supports locally hosted language models, including those served through Ollama, so teams can adopt conversational analytics without handing data to an outside AI service. The problem: AI that sends data elsewhere Conversational BI works by passing a user’s question, schema details and sometimes result data to a language model. If that model is run by an external provider, the information travels beyond the company’s walls. For regulated sectors, that raises concerns about privacy, data residency and audit readiness. The solution: bring your own model Helical Insight’s AI analytics module lets customers choose and host their own model. Paired with an on-premises installation, the full path from question to answer can stay within the organization’s network. Key facts Works with self-hosted models, including Ollama running on CPU or GPU servers Installs on-premises, in private cloud or in hybrid setups, including Docker and Kubernetes Role-based access, row-level security, SSO and multi-tenancy for controlled data access AI semantic layer for consistent business definitions Dashboards, paginated reports and embedded analytics in the same platform Full-featured [Community Edition](https://www.helicalinsight.com/community-edition/) with source code on GitHub, so security teams can inspect it “Our users in healthcare, finance and public-sector environments told us the same thing: they want flexibility of AI analytics, but the data cannot leave,” said Nikhilesh Tiwari, Co-founder, Helical Insight. “With a local model and an on-premises platform, they no longer have to choose between modern analytics and their security requirements.” Security remains a shared responsibility Helical Insight advises customers to pair local AI with sound controls: read-only database accounts, row-level permissions, encrypted logs with defined retention, and testing against prompt injection. Getting started Teams can download the platform at [helicalinsight.com/register](https://www.helicalinsight.com/register/), and get started. Required document and videos are present on the website. Community version can be download from github. Infra & Chips.content: [IBM Newsroom](index.php) # All press releases # llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale • llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads. • llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads [1] and three times greater output throughput. [2] Oct 20, 2026 ![](/image/iso_banner.png) **SAN JOSE, C.A., OCT. 20, 2026** – Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. The deal brings together a UK-registered engineering and project partner and a UK-registered systems business on an African data infrastructure project aimed at AI workloads. It also puts Nvidia's latest server architecture at the centre of the first announced phase. The 20MW site is planned near Casablanca, Morocco, and forms part of the larger Nexus AI Factory programme, which has a total planned size of 180MW. **Project scope** The initial 20MW facility is a substantial build in its own right, even before the wider campus is considered. Set within a 180MW scheme, it points to a multi-stage approach to AI-focused data centre construction in North Africa. The use of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 architecture suggests the site is intended for intensive AI computing rather than conventional enterprise hosting alone. Large AI data centres are increasingly designed around tightly integrated compute clusters, dense power delivery and specialist cooling systems, making design and delivery more complex than for standard colocation developments. Renewable energy is another notable feature of the outline released by the companies. Power sourcing has become a central issue for AI data centre developers as model training and inference workloads increase electricity demand and intensify scrutiny of grid access, cost and emissions. **Regional angle** For UK readers, the relevance lies in the role of two UK-registered companies in a major overseas infrastructure project. British technology, engineering and advisory firms have increasingly looked to international data centre markets as demand for AI infrastructure outpaces available supply in established hubs. Morocco has attracted growing attention as a location for digital infrastructure because of its position between European, African and Middle Eastern markets, as well as its renewable energy ambitions. Developers have also examined the country's potential to match power availability with rising demand for regional cloud and AI services. The project near Casablanca reflects a broader pattern in which AI infrastructure investment is no longer confined to traditional data centre centres in Western Europe and North America. Developers are instead assessing sites where land, energy strategy and regional connectivity may support large-scale computing estates. **Technology focus** Nvidia's newest AI systems have become a key reference point for developers pitching large compute sites to customers and investors. Infra & Chips.content: UPDATED 08:00 EDT / OCTOBER 20 2026 ### IBM-backed llm-d framework adds controls for running AI models in-house by Paul Gillin IBM Corp. and several other contributors to the open-source llm-d project are releasing version 1.0 of their distributed artificial intelligence inference framework, adding operational controls intended to help enterprises run large models reliably on their own infrastructure. The release, announced ahead of the PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose today and tomorrow, focuses on managing competing workloads, maintaining service during upgrades and improving hardware efficiency as AI agents generate growing volumes of model requests. Built for Kubernetes, llm-d coordinates model serving across computing infrastructure. IBM, its Red Hat subsidiary and Google LLC are its lead maintainers. They co-founded the project last year with CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia Corp. Other contributors include Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Cisco Systems Inc., Hugging Face Inc., Intel Corp. and Mistral AI SAS. The project offers organizations seeking more control over inference costs and infrastructure choices a way to reduce dependence on a single model provider, cloud or hardware platform. “At IBM Research, we are seeing that open large language models and llm-d can greatly lower the costs of inference in computationally demanding problems such as designing hardware for quantum error correction, helping achieve a 11.8X efficiency advantage,” Ruchir Puri, IBM Research’s chief scientist, vice president of IBM’s Technology & Technical Community and IBM Fellow, wrote in e-mailed comments. “Llm-d 1.0 extends these savings by delivering the operational readiness needed for enterprises to extract more out of their computational capacity.” The project is focused on what happens after deployment. A production inference service must handle changing traffic, hardware failures, software updates and users competing for resources while maintaining acceptable response times. Version 1.0 adds support for quality of service across multiple tenants, zero-downtime operations and serving patterns tailored to AI agents. Flow controls and prioritization are designed to keep bursts of agent activity from overwhelming services that require fast responses, such as coding assistants used by people. The release “adds the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable [application programming interface], multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure and upgrades that don’t interrupt operations,” said Carlos Costa, distinguished engineer at IBM Research and a project co-founder and lead maintainer. Workloads can behave differently even when they reach models through the same endpoint. An agent may issue many requests, pause to use an external tool and return for additional model calls. The framework can keep requests directed to appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns, increasing opportunities to reuse previously processed context. That matters because agents repeatedly consult the same code, documents, instructions and conversation history while completing assignments. A routing system directs requests toward replicas that already hold relevant cached context. Another capability moves cached information among graphics processing unit memory, CPU memory and storage, preserving reusable information when GPU capacity becomes constrained. These techniques were previously available, but version 1.0 integrates them with operational controls, along with methods that separate prompt processing from response generation, optimize work batches and distribute large mixture-of-experts models across accelerators. IBM cited a recent agentic coding test in which the framework’s router captured 97% of available cache reuse. The release, announced ahead of the PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose today and tomorrow, focuses on managing competing workloads, maintaining service during upgrades and improving hardware efficiency as AI agents generate growing volumes of model requests. Built for Kubernetes, llm-d coordinates model serving across computing infrastructure. IBM, its Red Hat subsidiary and Google LLC are its lead maintainers. They co-founded the project last year with CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia Corp. Other contributors include Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Cisco Systems Inc., Hugging Face Inc., Intel Corp. and Mistral AI SAS. The project offers organizations seeking more control over inference costs and infrastructure choices a way to reduce dependence on a single model provider, cloud or hardware platform. “At IBM Research, we are seeing that open large language models and llm-d can greatly lower the costs of inference in computationally demanding problems such as designing hardware for quantum error correction, helping achieve a 11.8X efficiency advantage,” Ruchir Puri, IBM Research’s chief scientist, vice president of IBM’s Technology & Technical Community and IBM Fellow, wrote in e-mailed comments. “Llm-d 1.0 extends these savings by delivering the operational readiness needed for enterprises to extract more out of their computational capacity.” The project is focused on what happens after deployment. A production inference service must handle changing traffic, hardware failures, software updates and users competing for resources while maintaining acceptable response times. Version 1.0 adds support for quality of service across multiple tenants, zero-downtime operations and serving patterns tailored to AI agents. Flow controls and prioritization are designed to keep bursts of agent activity from overwhelming services that require fast responses, such as coding assistants used by people. The release “adds the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable [application programming interface], multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure and upgrades that don’t interrupt operations,” said Carlos Costa, distinguished engineer at IBM Research and a project co-founder and lead maintainer. Workloads can behave differently even when they reach models through the same endpoint. An agent may issue many requests, pause to use an external tool and return for additional model calls. The framework can keep requests directed to appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns, increasing opportunities to reuse previously processed context. That matters because agents repeatedly consult the same code, documents, instructions and conversation history while completing assignments. A routing system directs requests toward replicas that already hold relevant cached context. Another capability moves cached information among graphics processing unit memory, CPU memory and storage, preserving reusable information when GPU capacity becomes constrained. These techniques were previously available, but version 1.0 integrates them with operational controls, along with methods that separate prompt processing from response generation, optimize work batches and distribute large mixture-of-experts models across accelerators. IBM cited a recent agentic coding test in which the framework’s router captured 97% of available cache reuse.
